title: Build a Private Agent Network for Your Company
description: Deploy a private Pilot Protocol network inside your organization. No data leaves your infrastructure. See the technical details.
seoTitle: Build a Private Agent Network | Pilot Protocol Blog
author: Pilot Protocol editorial team

children.text: Your company is deploying AI agents. They process customer data, access internal APIs, and coordinate decisions across departments. The question every CISO asks:
where does the data go?

With cloud-hosted agent platforms, the answer is uncomfortable. Agent communication routes through third-party infrastructure -- vendor servers, managed message brokers, cloud relay services. Even with TLS, the relay operator can see metadata: which agents are talking, how often, and how much data is flowing. For regulated industries -- healthcare, finance, defense, legal -- this is a compliance problem. For any company that takes data sovereignty seriously, it is a strategic risk.
Pilot Protocol can run
entirely on your infrastructure

. The rendezvous server, the beacon, and every agent daemon run on machines you control. Point the daemons at your own registry, turn off the default outbound feeds, and no agent traffic or metadata goes to a third party. This post walks through a complete self-hosted deployment, from architecture to production hardening.
Why Your Agent Network Should Be Private
There are three reasons companies deploy private agent networks instead of using public infrastructure.
Data Sovereignty

When agents exchange data through a broker or cloud relay, traffic transits infrastructure you do not own. Even when payloads are encrypted, the infrastructure operator may observe routing metadata such as who communicates, when, and how often. Organizations handling personal or regulated data must assess which privacy, security, contracting, and deployment obligations apply to their role and environment.

In a self-hosted private Pilot deployment, the registry and beacon run on infrastructure you control. Encrypted tunnels prefer direct paths and use the self-hosted beacon as a ciphertext relay when necessary. The coordination layer can observe connection metadata, but the standard encrypted profile does not expose tunnel payload contents to it.
Zero Cloud Dependency

Cloud-hosted agent platforms create vendor lock-in. If the platform has an outage, your agents stop communicating. If the vendor changes pricing, you pay or migrate. If the vendor shuts down, you start from scratch. For a detailed analysis of these risks, see
Run an Agent Network Without Cloud Dependency

A self-hosted Pilot network needs no outside service. The stack is a handful of pure-Go binaries — the daemon and CLI on each node, and the rendezvous server (registry + beacon) you run centrally. No package managers, no runtime dependencies, no license servers.
Audit

When auditors ask "how do your agents communicate and who can access the communication channel," a private deployment gives a simple answer: all communication occurs over encrypted P2P tunnels within your network, coordinated by infrastructure you control, logged by systems you own. Pilot does not make a deployment compliant with any standard; it keeps the communication path inside the boundary you already audit.
Architecture Overview
A private Pilot Protocol deployment consists of three components:
Rendezvous server
-- runs the registry (port 9000) and beacon (port 9001) on a machine with a static internal IP. This is the only component that must be reachable by all agents.
Agent daemon
-- runs on each machine that hosts an agent. Handles tunnel management, encryption, NAT traversal, and connection multiplexing.
CLI (pilotctl)
-- the management tool. Used to create networks, join agents, configure trust, and monitor the deployment.
Here is how these components connect in a typical company deployment:

fields.code:
# Private network architecture
#
#   +---------------------+
#   |  Rendezvous Server  |
#   |  (registry :9000)   |
#   |  (beacon   :9001)   |
#   |  10.0.1.10          |
#   +----------+----------+
#              |
#     +--------+--------+
#     |        |        |
#  +--+--+  +--+--+  +--+--+
#  |Agent|  |Agent|  |Agent|
#  | A   |  | B   |  | C   |
#  |10.0 |  |10.0 |  |10.0 |
#  |.1.20|  |.1.30|  |.2.40|
#  +-----+  +-----+  +-----+
#
# Agents connect to registry over TCP :9000
# Agents tunnel to each other over UDP
# Beacon :9001 coordinates hole-punch if subnets differ

children.text: The rendezvous server is lightweight -- it stores agent registrations in memory and persists them to a JSON file on disk. It does not process or inspect agent traffic. Once two agents have resolved each other's endpoints through the registry, all subsequent data flows directly between them over encrypted UDP tunnels.
Step 1: Deploy the Rendezvous Server
The rendezvous server runs the registry and beacon as a single process. Choose a machine with a static IP that all agents can reach. This can be a dedicated VM, a bare-metal server, or a container.
The installer does not include the rendezvous server. Build it from its own repository (Go, no cgo):

fields.code:
# Build the rendezvous server from source
git clone https://github.com/pilot-protocol/rendezvous
cd rendezvous && go build -o pilot-rendezvous ./cmd/rendezvous

# Start it: registry on TCP :9000, beacon on UDP :9001
# The admin token is what lets you create networks; without it, creation is disabled
export PILOT_ADMIN_TOKEN=<long-random-secret>
./pilot-rendezvous -registry-addr :9000 -beacon-addr :9001 -store /var/lib/pilot/registry.json

children.text: For production, run the rendezvous server as a systemd service:

fields.code:
# /etc/systemd/system/pilot-rendezvous.service
# (/etc/pilot/rendezvous.env holds PILOT_ADMIN_TOKEN=<long-random-secret>)
[Unit]
Description=Pilot Protocol Rendezvous Server
After=network.target

[Service]
Type=simple
EnvironmentFile=/etc/pilot/rendezvous.env
ExecStart=/usr/local/bin/pilot-rendezvous -registry-addr :9000 -beacon-addr :9001 -store /var/lib/pilot/registry.json
Restart=always
RestartSec=5
User=pilot
Group=pilot

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target

sudo systemctl enable pilot-rendezvous
sudo systemctl start pilot-rendezvous

children.text: The registry persists state to a JSON snapshot when you pass
-store <path>
(e.g.
/var/lib/pilot/registry.json
); with no
-store
it keeps state in memory only. On restart, it reloads all agent registrations from this file. Configure your backup system to include this path.
Firewall rules:

The rendezvous server needs TCP port 9000 (registry) and UDP port 9001 (beacon) open to all agent machines. No other inbound ports are required. The server does not need internet access -- it runs entirely within your network.
Step 2: Start Agent Daemons
On each machine that will run an agent, deploy the Pilot daemon. The daemon handles tunnel management, encryption, and communication with the rendezvous server.

fields.code:
# Install pilotctl, pilot-daemon and pilot-updater to ~/.pilot/bin
curl -fsSL https://pilotprotocol.network/install.sh | sh

# Start the daemon, pointing to your private rendezvous server.
# The two empty URLs turn off the default MOTD feed and telemetry.
~/.pilot/bin/pilot-daemon -registry 10.0.1.10:9000 -beacon 10.0.1.10:9001 \
  -identity ~/.pilot/identity.json -motd-feed-url "" -telemetry-url ""

# Point pilotctl at the same registry (it is used for network admin commands)
pilotctl config --set registry=10.0.1.10:9000

children.text: The installer also starts
pilot-updater
, which checks GitHub for new releases. Stop that service and update by hand if these machines must make no outside calls.
The daemon generates a cryptographic identity (Ed25519 keypair) on first run and stores it at
~/.pilot/identity.json

. This identity is permanent -- it persists across restarts and is used for all trust operations. Back up this file; losing it means the agent gets a new identity and must re-establish all trust relationships.

For machines on the same subnet as the rendezvous server, the daemon will register its local IP as the endpoint. For machines on different subnets, the daemon uses STUN discovery through the beacon to determine its reachable endpoint. The beacon coordinates hole-punching for cross-subnet communication automatically.
Step 3: Create a Private Network
Pilot Protocol supports multiple isolated networks on the same infrastructure. Each network gets a 16-bit network ID, and agents on different networks cannot see or communicate with each other.

fields.code:
# Create a private network (needs the registry's admin token)
PILOT_ADMIN_TOKEN=<long-random-secret> pilotctl network create --name corp-net

# Output:
# created network 1: corp-net (join_rule=open, enterprise=false)

children.text: The network name is a human-readable label. Internally, the registry assigns a 16-bit network ID. All agents that join this network receive addresses with this network prefix, isolating them from agents on other networks (including the default backbone network 0).
Step 4: Join Agents and Set Visibility
With the network created, join each agent and configure its visibility.

fields.code:
# On Agent A: join the corp-net network
pilotctl network join 1   # network_id, not a name

# Register a human-readable hostname
pilotctl set-hostname "data-processor"

# Set visibility to private (this is the default)
pilotctl set-private

# Verify registration: hostname, address, node ID, peers
pilotctl info
pilotctl network list

children.text: Repeat this on each agent machine, choosing a descriptive hostname for each:

fields.code:
# On Agent B
pilotctl network join 1
pilotctl set-hostname "model-runner"

# On Agent C
pilotctl network join 1
pilotctl set-hostname "orchestrator"

children.text: With visibility set to private, these agents are registered with the rendezvous server but
invisible to everyone outside the network
. A private agent's endpoint resolves only for nodes that trust it or share a network with it. This is the foundation of Pilot's
invisible-by-default trust model
Step 5: Establish Trust Between Agents
Agents must trust each other before they can exchange data. This is done through a cryptographic handshake signed with each agent's Ed25519 keypair.

fields.code:
# On the orchestrator: request trust with data-processor and model-runner
pilotctl handshake data-processor "Orchestrator requesting secure channel"
pilotctl handshake model-runner "Orchestrator needs to delegate inference"

# Members of the same private network are approved automatically.
# A peer that shares no network approves by hand on its side:
pilotctl approve orchestrator

children.text: After mutual approval, both agents can resolve each other's endpoints and establish encrypted tunnels. The trust state is persisted to disk and survives daemon restarts.
Automatic Approval
For larger deployments, managing individual handshakes becomes impractical. The daemon has two built-in approval rules:
Shared network.
A handshake from a member of a private network you also belong to is approved automatically. This is the default; there is nothing to configure.
Approve everything.
pilotctl daemon start --trust-auto-approve
(or
-trust-auto-approve
on
pilot-daemon
) approves every incoming handshake. Use it only on a registry where every node is yours.

Networks are the unit of policy. In a department-level deployment, you might give each department its own network, so approval is automatic within the department and cross-department trust needs a manual approval. For a deeper exploration of trust architecture, see
Secure Agent Communication with Zero Trust
Step 6: Bridge to Legacy Systems
Not every system in your organization will run a Pilot agent. Legacy services -- REST APIs, databases, monitoring systems -- still use traditional TCP/IP. The Pilot
gateway
bridges the two worlds. It is an optional companion binary,
pilot-gateway
, that is not in the release tarballs (see
pilot-protocol/gateway
), and it needs root.

The gateway assigns a local IP from a subnet (10.4.0.0/16 by default) to each Pilot address, adds it as a loopback alias, and listens on the mapped ports, proxying traffic between local TCP clients and Pilot tunnels.

fields.code:
# Start the gateway on the orchestrator machine, mapping two agents
sudo pilotctl extras gateway start --ports 80 1:0001.0000.0001 1:0001.0000.0002
# mapped 10.4.0.1 → 1:0001.0000.0001   (data-processor)
# mapped 10.4.0.2 → 1:0001.0000.0002   (model-runner)

# Now legacy tools can reach Pilot agents via local IPs
curl http://10.4.0.1:80/api/status
# Routes through Pilot tunnel to data-processor, port 80

children.text: This means existing monitoring tools (Prometheus, Grafana), CI/CD pipelines, and management scripts can interact with Pilot agents without modification.
Port mapping:
The gateway listens on the same port numbers that the remote Pilot agent exposes. If
data-processor
runs an HTTP service on port 80, the gateway listens on
. On Linux, ports below 1024 require root. The gateway automatically adds loopback aliases using
ip addr add
on Linux or
ifconfig lo0 alias
on macOS.
Security Hardening
A private deployment provides network-level isolation, but production hardening requires additional measures.
TLS for Registry Connections

Agent-to-registry communication uses TCP. In a private network, this traffic stays within your infrastructure, but you should still encrypt it. Pilot supports TLS with certificate pinning for registry connections:

fields.code:
# Generate a TLS certificate for the rendezvous server
openssl req -x509 -newkey ec -pkeyopt ec_paramgen_curve:prime256v1 \
  -keyout registry-key.pem -out registry-cert.pem -days 365 -nodes \
  -subj "/CN=pilot-rendezvous"

# Start rendezvous with TLS
./pilot-rendezvous -registry-addr :9000 -beacon-addr :9001 \
  -tls -tls-cert registry-cert.pem -tls-key registry-key.pem

# On agents: pin the registry certificate
./pilot-daemon -registry 10.0.1.10:9000 -beacon 10.0.1.10:9001 \
  -registry-tls -registry-fingerprint <hex-sha256>

children.text: Certificate pinning means agents will refuse to connect to a registry that presents a different certificate. This prevents man-in-the-middle attacks even if an attacker compromises your DNS or ARP tables.
IPC Socket Permissions
The daemon exposes a Unix domain socket at
/tmp/pilot.sock
for CLI communication. In a multi-user environment, restrict access to this socket:

fields.code:
# Set socket permissions to owner-only
chmod 600 /tmp/pilot.sock

# Run the daemon as a dedicated user
sudo useradd -r -s /usr/sbin/nologin pilot
sudo -u pilot ./pilot-daemon -registry 10.0.1.10:9000 -beacon 10.0.1.10:9001

children.text: Per-Port Accept Rules

By default, a Pilot agent accepts connections on all ports it has listeners for. In a hardened deployment, you can restrict which ports are allowed on the network with a port whitelist in the network policy:

fields.code:
# Allow only the echo, stdio, and messaging ports on network 1 (needs the admin token)
pilotctl network policy 1 --allowed-ports 7,1000,1001
# updated policy for network 1
# Member daemons refuse connections to any port off the list

children.text: Per-port accept rules provide defense in depth. Even if an attacker compromises one agent and establishes trust, they can only access the specific ports that the network policy permits.
Structured Logging and Audit Trail
The daemon logs with Go's
slog
package. Start it with
-log-format json
and trust events, refused connections, and errors come out as JSON lines with machine-parseable fields:

Ship these logs to your SIEM (Splunk, Elastic, Datadog) as an audit trail. The rendezvous server can also export its own audit events (Splunk HEC, CEF/syslog, or JSON). The structured format makes it straightforward to create alerts on trust changes, failed connections, and unusual traffic patterns.
High Availability

The rendezvous server is a single point of coordination (not a single point of failure for data -- agent-to-agent tunnels continue working if the registry goes down temporarily). For production deployments that require HA, Pilot supports hot-standby replication.

fields.code:
# Primary rendezvous server
./pilot-rendezvous -registry-addr :9000 -beacon-addr :9001 \
  -store /var/lib/pilot/registry.json -repl-token <shared-token>

# Standby rendezvous server
./pilot-rendezvous -registry-addr :9000 -beacon-addr :9001 \
  -standby primary.internal:9000 -repl-token <shared-token>

children.text: The primary streams each change to the standby as it happens (with a full snapshot when a standby falls behind) and sends a heartbeat every 10 seconds. If the primary fails, a manual failover promotes the standby. Existing agent tunnels continue functioning during the failover window -- only new registrations and resolves are affected.
Production Deployment Checklist
Before going live, verify each item:
Rendezvous server:
Running as systemd service, TLS enabled, persistence directory backed up
Firewall rules:
TCP 9000 and UDP 9001 open from all agent subnets to rendezvous server
Agent daemons:
Running as systemd services, identity files backed up, pointing to private registry
Network isolation:
Agents joined to private network, visibility set to private
Trust:
Agents that work together share a network, or their handshakes are approved
IPC security:
Daemon running as dedicated user, socket permissions restricted
Port policy:
Each network allows only the ports its agents use
Logging:
Structured logs shipping to SIEM, alerts configured for trust changes
HA:
Standby rendezvous server configured and tested
Outbound calls:
MOTD feed and telemetry off, updater stopped if machines must make no outside calls
Gateway:
Configured for any legacy system integration needed
What You Get
A private Pilot Protocol deployment gives your organization:
Data sovereignty
-- agent traffic and coordination stay on your infrastructure
End-to-end encryption
-- X25519 + AES-256-GCM between every pair of agents, with the rendezvous server never seeing payload data
Cryptographic identity
-- every agent has an Ed25519 keypair, trust is explicit and auditable
No cloud dependency
-- the entire stack runs on your machines, and the default outbound calls (MOTD feed, telemetry, updater) can be turned off
Legacy compatibility
-- the optional gateway bridges Pilot agents to existing HTTP/TCP systems without modification
Your agents communicate freely within your network. Nothing leaves your control. And when the deployment grows from 3 agents to 300, the only thing that changes is the number of daemons you run.
